summary:
Neil Dwyer, CTO of Gabber, shares lessons from deploying Orpheus, an open-source real-time text-to-speech model, for consumer AI persona applications. Gabber's mission is making real-time synchronous AI ubiquitous within 2-5 years, targeting consumer use cases (AI girlfriends, NPCs, therapists, toys) rather than enterprise call centers. The core challenge is cost: existing voice platforms charge $5+/hour, prohibitive for most consumer apps needing near-free economics. Orpheus, based on Llama 3B pre-trained on 100,000 hours of voice and text, outputs 24kHz snack tokens at ~85 tokens/second, requiring 90-100 tokens/second throughput for real-time playback.

One-shot voice cloning underperforms due to Orpheus's limited pre-training data (100k vs. 1M+ hours for commercial models), so Gabber uses LoRA fine-tunes (rank 16, alpha 32, all projections) with 10-30 minutes of data. A major latency discovery was "head of line silence" — default voice "Tara" has 600ms of silence from training data. On L40S GPUs (~100 tokens/sec), filtering only saves ~10% since generation barely exceeds real-time. Fine-tuning away silence reduced P50 latency to ~100ms, critical within the latency budget where endpointing snooze periods (0.5-1.5s acceptable) allow LLM pre-generation.

For infrastructure, Gabber uses vLLM with batch inference supporting multiple LoRAs per GPU. FP16 was slower than real-time on L40S, so FP8 dynamic quantization (zero-config, automatic scaling) achieved 105 tokens/sec on base voices and 95 tokens/sec on LoRA voices with batch size 10 — sufficient for margins. Load balancing uses a consistent hash ring: servers are hashed multiple times as virtual nodes, requests hashed with the same algorithm route to the nearest server. This enables sticky sessions (LoRAs are 100-200MB, must stay in memory), supports streaming input for arbitrarily long generation, and allows adding popular LoRAs to more servers without major rebalancing. The architecture routes WebRTC client connections through a backend that queries Redis for GPU assignment, then proxies via TCP to the correct GPU within the same data center's private network. Neil concludes that Gabber's scrappy team proved self-hosted voice models are achievable, crediting the open-source ecosystem: Canopy Labs (Orpheus, built on Llama and Snack), LiveKit (WebRTC infrastructure), vLLM, and Swix.

sections.title: Speaker Background and Gabber Introduction
sections.summary: Neil Dwyer introduces himself and his career in real-time media: Bebo (game streaming, acquired by Amazon), Uber, a multiplayer gaming startup with his brother, LiveKit (where he built the Agents platform), and now Gabber. Gabber provides real-time infrastructure for AI personas focused on consumer use cases, with building blocks like voice memory, video inputs, and tool calling. Neil differentiates Gabber by targeting consumer apps rather than enterprise call-center scenarios, predicting real-time synchronous AI will become as ubiquitous as websites within 2-5 years.

sections.title: Cost Problem and Orpheus Model
sections.summary: Neil explains that existing voice platforms charging $5+/hour only work for monetized consumer apps like AI girlfriends with credit systems; most consumer use cases need near-free economics. Gabber needed to bring voice model hosting in-house. Orpheus was the first good open-source real-time streaming voice model, based on Llama 3B, pre-trained on 100,000 hours of voice and text data, outputting 24kHz snack tokens at ~85 tokens/second. Going viral on Twitter after deploying Orpheus on an H100 was a turning point for the company.

sections.title: Voice Cloning with LoRA Fine-Tunes
sections.summary: One-shot cloning doesn't work well with Orpheus due to limited pre-training data (100k hours vs. 1M+ for zero-shot emergent behavior). Gabber uses LoRA fine-tunes (rank 16, alpha 32, all projections) with 10-30 minutes of training data. Neil demonstrates a clone of his brother Jack's voice trained on 10 minutes of data over 5 epochs (overfit but functional), showing emotive qualities like capturing sadness from language cues.

sections.title: Latency and Head of Line Silence
sections.summary: Four latency factors: time to first token, tokens per second, network latency, and head-of-line silence. The latter was the biggest issue — default Orpheus voice 'Tara' has 600ms of silence from voice actor training data. On L40S (~100 tokens/second), filtering silence only saves ~10% because generation barely exceeds real-time. Fine-tuning away the silence reduced P50 latency to ~100ms. This matters within the latency budget: endpointing snooze periods (ideally 0.5-1s, max ~1.5s) allow LLM pre-generation; Gabber starts TTS after 2 sentences for emotional context.

sections.title: Infrastructure: Batch Inference and vLLM
sections.summary: Gabber needed batch inference with multiple LoRAs on the same GPU and a single load balancer across multiple language-specific model deployments. vLLM provided batch inference with LoRA support. The FP16 Orpheus model was slower than real-time on L40S (worked on H100), so they adopted vLLM's FP8 dynamic quantization, which requires zero configuration and works automatically without calibration data. This achieved 105 tokens/second on non-fine-tuned voices and 95 tokens/second on LoRA voices with a batch of 10, well within margin requirements.

sections.title: Load Balancing with Consistent Hash Ring
sections.summary: LoRAs are 100-200MB depending on hyperparameters, so sticky sessions ensure requests land on a GPU with the LoRA already in memory. Gabber also needed streaming input support for cases where the LLM isn't done generating but audio should start, plus arbitrarily long generation for storytelling. These requirements mean the same GPU must serve an entire session. Gabber uses a consistent hash ring: servers are hashed multiple times as virtual nodes distributed around a ring; incoming requests are hashed with the same algorithm and routed to the nearest server. Removing a server only causes a few migrations, not full rebalancing. Popular clones can be scaled by appending the LoRA to additional servers without significant engineering work.

sections.title: System Architecture Overview
sections.summary: The architecture: a WebRTC backend terminates client connections, then uses WebSockets to communicate with GPUs. GPUs talk to Redis, which tracks request-to-GPU assignments. When a session starts, the WebRTC backend connects to any GPU, queries Redis for the correct GPU for that request, then proxies via TCP to the right GPU. This works because all GPUs are in the same data center on private networking, so TCP latency is negligible. Redis is acknowledged as not the best choice but sufficient at current scale; scaling beyond it would require additional investment.

sections.title: Conclusion and Open Source Shout-outs
sections.summary: Neil concludes that Gabber's scrappy team successfully hosted voice models on GPUs and managed the infrastructure, encouraging others that they can too. He credits the open-source ecosystem: Swix for support, Canopy Labs for creating Orpheus (built on Llama and Snack), LiveKit for WebRTC infrastructure (Gabber is a LiveKit alum), and vLLM as a notable open-source project. He emphasizes the ecosystem is greater than the sum of its parts.
